original_question: What notion of security should be used for noncommutative group-based cryptography: practicality, worst-case complexity, average-case complexity, generic complexity, or some other measure?
target_in_paper: Section 11, "Open Problems in Nonabelian Group Based Cryptography," General item 6: "what should be the measure of the security? (practicality, complexity, average case complexity, generic complexity?)"
correct_elements: The draft is aimed at the correct open problem in the paper and already preserves the paper's main candidate security measures: practicality, complexity, average-case complexity, and generic complexity. Recasting "complexity" as worst-case complexity is faithful to the nearby discussion in Section 9, where worst-case, average-case, and generic complexity are explicitly distinguished.
missing_details: The paper is asking this question in the specific setting of the non-commutative group-based schemes surveyed in the article, especially public key exchange, digital signature, and authentication protocols, not cryptography in full generality.

The intended notion of "complexity" needs to be unpacked using Section 9: worst-case complexity, average-case complexity, and generic-case complexity are distinct notions, and the point of the open problem is to decide which of them should govern security evaluation.

The security notion is tied to cryptanalysis of underlying group-theoretic search/decision problems used by the protocols, such as conjugacy/conjugator-search-type problems, rather than to an abstract information-theoretic notion of secrecy.

The paper's motivation includes the fact that some problems may be hard on some inputs but easy on most inputs; thus any stand-alone formulation should make explicit that the choice of security measure may depend on typical/random inputs or asymptotically generic inputs, not only worst-case instances.

The role of "practicality" should be made explicit: earlier platform-group discussion treats efficient normal forms, a solvable and practically computable word problem, and implementability as relevant criteria alongside hardness of the attack problem.

The paper does not supply a formal adversary model, a reduction-based security definition, a fixed probability distribution on inputs, or a single designated platform group, so a paper-faithful rewrite should not silently add any of those.

No ambient ring/field, variables, operator definitions, homogeneity assumptions, degree restrictions, nilpotency conditions, or quantifiers such as "for all sufficiently large m" are relevant here; the missing details are conceptual and cryptographic rather than algebraic.
refined_question: For the non-commutative group-based cryptographic schemes surveyed in this paper—particularly public key exchange, digital-signature, and authentication protocols based on group-theoretic search or decision problems—what should be taken as the primary measure of security: practical resistance to attacks, worst-case computational complexity of the underlying problem, average-case complexity with respect to the protocol's input generation, or generic-case complexity on asymptotically most inputs?
justification: The draft is targeting Section 11, General open problem 6 almost verbatim. The nearby context that sharpens it is Section 9, where the paper explicitly distinguishes worst-case, average-case, and generic complexity and explains why this distinction matters for cryptanalysis; Section 1 also announces asymptotic-density methods as tools for evaluating cryptosystems. Earlier platform-group discussion explains why "practicality" appears in the list at all: a useful platform must admit efficient normal forms and a feasible word problem, while the associated attack problem should remain hard. So the paper-faithful sharpening is not to broaden the question, but to state explicitly that the issue is which security metric should govern evaluation of the surveyed non-commutative group-based schemes built from group-theoretic problems.
